terms.definition: A range computed from sample data by a procedure with a stated conditional success rate, reported as a lower and an upper limit in the units of a defined population quantity. It gives the parameter values that the sample is compatible with under the stated sampling and analysis model, and it says nothing about where any individual observation sits.

The stated conditional success rate of the procedure that produced an interval: the long-run proportion of intervals that would contain the fixed parameter if independent sampling and analysis were repeated under the procedure's assumptions. It is a property of the method, not a feeling of certainty, and it does not repair bias or guarantee generalisation beyond the defined population.

The single value a sample gives for a quantity you want to know, such as the 9.0 mg/dL difference this study measured. It is the best guess the sample supports and it carries no information about how far off it might be.

A fixed unknown quantity belonging to the population a sample was drawn from, such as the true difference in average fasting glucose between two ways of eating. It has one value, that value does not change when you sample, and no study observes it directly.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-010 defines a model parameter as a quantity an author sets or adjusts inside a scientific model to make it behave. The statistical sense used here is the opposite arrangement: nobody sets it and nobody can read it off, because it belongs to the population and the study exists to estimate it. Both senses are standard and the concept scene bridges them where the word first appears in this lesson.

terms.definition: The standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples of the same size: how far the study's number would move if the whole study were run again on fresh people. It sets the unit an interval is measured in.

alignment.note: PREM-STA-006 owns this term and its derivation from the sampling distribution, and this lesson keeps that meaning unchanged. Nothing new is added to the definition here; the standard error is taken as an input and turned into the width of an interval. A learner who cannot say what the standard error describes is sent back to that lesson in the opening scene.

terms.definition: The distribution of an estimate across every sample of a given size that could have been drawn under a stated model. For an unbiased estimator it is centred on the fixed true parameter, not on the estimate from one observed sample, and its spread is the standard error.

alignment.note: PREM-STA-006 owns this term and this lesson keeps its meaning unchanged. This lesson uses it only to distinguish the fixed parameter from the estimates and intervals that vary across repeated samples; it does not centre a hypothetical repeat-study distribution on the observed estimate.

terms.definition: Half the width of a confidence interval: the multiplier times the standard error, in the units of the estimate. It is the distance you reach out from the estimate in each direction, and doubling it gives the interval's width.

How tightly a study has pinned down the quantity it set out to estimate, read directly from the width of its interval. A narrow interval is a precise result and a wide one is an imprecise result, whatever the estimate at the centre happens to be.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-006 owns measurement precision, which is how closely repeated measurements of the same thing by the same instrument agree. The sense used here is a property of a whole study's estimate, and the two are related without being the same: a precise instrument reduces the spread that feeds the standard error, but sample size moves this kind of precision and instrument quality alone cannot. The width scene keeps the two apart where they meet.

terms.definition: The number an effect would take if the two groups being compared were the same: zero for a difference between two averages. Checking whether an interval contains it is the first thing most readers do, and it answers only whether the direction is supported.

Describes the family of statistical methods, confidence intervals among them, whose statements are read as frequencies across imagined repeats of the same study. A frequentist method reports how often a procedure would behave in a given way and never attaches a probability to the fixed parameter itself.

A curve shaped like the normal one but with slightly heavier tails, used in place of it when the spread of the data had to be estimated from the same sample as the estimate. Its multipliers are a little larger than the normal ones, and the difference shrinks as the sample grows.

A count of how many numbers in a sample were still free to vary once the quantities already computed from it are held fixed. Comparing two groups of 30 leaves 58, because two group averages were computed from the 60 readings before any spread could be measured, and it is the number that selects a row of the t table.

The values of the unknown parameter that a study's data do not argue against at a stated level under the analysis model. Describing an interval this way keeps the statement about the data, preserves the model conditions, and avoids assigning a probability to the parameter.
